idiom_name: immutable rule-table snapshot + atomic publish from a control channel
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep routing policy in a rule base that can be replaced as a whole (table, configuration document, database view or rules engine), publish a validated new rule set atomically, and let every message read exactly one snapshot so it is routed by one generation of rules. Give the router an explicit unmatched case that routes to a dead-letter or default destination, and record which rule matched so an incident can be reconstructed. What replaces the classic structure in most modern stacks is a qualified registry plus an atomic swap (atomic pointer, OptionsMonitor, ArcSwap, StateFlow); the full EIP structure - router, rules base, control channel, announcing destinations - is still justified when the rule source is shared across routers or maintained by non-developers, and a rules engine is justified when conditions are complex or composed by domain experts.
pitfalls: Publishing rules by editing a live table entry by entry: messages can be routed by a half-applied rule set - publish whole snapshots.
No unmatched-message policy: unmatched traffic is dropped silently instead of landing in a dead-letter destination somebody monitors.
A rule base that names destinations the router cannot verify, so a typo or a decommissioned endpoint becomes a black hole.

Regex engine version skew (e.g. Envoy v2 → v3 regex routing): a rule that worked in staging silently drops all matching traffic in production because the engine was changed beneath it — pin the engine version or avoid regex routing rules.

Publishing individual rule deltas instead of whole snapshots: concurrent readers can observe a half-applied rule set where one destination has been removed but its replacement is not yet visible, causing traffic to fall through to the unroutable handler.

Over-permissive automation on the control channel: a routing automation that treats 'no matching rule' as 'export everything' (Cloudflare BGP leak pattern) can advertise internal destinations externally — scope every automation term explicitly.

Unbounded per-message rule evaluation: a linear scan of thousands of rules or a recursive expression that keeps adding conditions produces latency that scales with traffic, not with the number of destinations.
Rule evaluation that is non-terminating: a DynamicRouter expression that never returns null (or an infinite loop in a bean) routes messages forever — always enforce an evaluation hop limit.

Wrong move: pushing an unvalidated route through the admin/actuator endpoint and refreshing -> a single invalid route definition can fail the whole refresh and take all existing routes down (Spring Cloud Gateway gh-600) -> validate predicates, filters and destination reachability first and swap only a fully valid snapshot, keeping the last-known-good set on failure.

Wrong move: treating runtime-socket changes as the source of truth (e.g. HAProxy Runtime API add/set server) -> the changes are in-memory only and vanish on the next reload or restart, so a crash reverts to a stale routing table -> persist every runtime change through a layer that re-applies it (Data Plane API, state file, or the owning control channel).

Wrong move: propagating rule snapshots to every replica with no size or complexity bound -> a rule file that grows unbounded exceeds a runtime limit on the router and fails the whole data path, not just the new rules (Cloudflare 18-Nov-2025 outage: an oversized feature file caused global 500s) -> bound snapshot size, validate against the router's runtime limits, and stage the rollout instead of global-at-once.
